paper.page: CertEx: Exact Visual Retrieval at Scale by Certified Exclusion Dongfang Zhao Tacoma School of Engineering & Technology and eScience Institute University of Washington dzhao@uw.edu Abstract Exact k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) search over image de- scriptors and embeddings underlies visual retrieval, near- duplicate detection, the evaluation of learned representa- tions, and increasingly the memory of LLM agents. How- ever, exhaustive search computes every distance at full pre- cision, whereas approximate indexes return recall below one. We observe that exact search only needs a proof that each excluded vector cannot be a neighbor. Because such a proof only has to be conservative, it can be checked in low precision, much as the retina examines the whole scene at low resolution. We call this principle certified exclusion and realize it in an exact kNN method for GPUs, which we call CertEx. Specifically, CertEx stores a lower-bounding pro- jection of each vector in half precision and folds a round- ing certificate into the same tensor-core dot product, so that only the few vectors that the test keeps need exact distances. We prove that CertEx returns the exact kNN of every query. On sixteen datasets with up to 100M vectors, CertEx is ex- act for every query at 7.1× to 18.0× the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 and outperforms quan- tized and graph indexes whenever every query must be ex- act. 1 Introduction Exact kNN search over large collections of visual features is a basic operation whose errors propagate into the tasks built on top of it. For instance, image retrieval ranks database de- scriptors such as SIFT [42] by their distance to a query de- scriptor, so that a missed neighbor removes a relevant image from the ranked list. Similarly, near-duplicate detection in web-scale training corpora such as LAION [58] compares every image embedding with its nearest neighbors [54], so that a missed neighbor keeps a duplicate pair in the train- ing data. Likewise, the kNN classifier that evaluates self- supervised representations [12, 50, 70] reports the search er- ror together with the quality of the representation whenever its neighbors are approximate. Moreover, LLMs and agents increasingly read long contexts and memories by nearest- neighbor search [4, 11, 34, 38, 39, 67, 69, 71], so that a missed neighbor drops a relevant memory. Finally, every benchmark of approximate search measures recall against exact neighbors and therefore inherits any error of the ex- haustive search that computes them. Existing systems respond to the cost of exact search in two ways, both of which leave a gap. First, exhaustive search on GPUs [18, 35] computes every query-to-vector distance at full precision. The throughput of exhaustive search is therefore bounded by one full-precision distance per vector, and its capacity is bounded by device memory, which must hold every vector at full precision. Second, approximate indexes based on quantization [22, 28, 37] or proximity graphs [43, 49, 63] are much faster. However, these indexes trade recall for speed by design and rely on an index that must be built before the first query and repaired when the collection changes [74]. Practitioners therefore choose between exact results at high cost and fast results whose errors are not controlled per query. To close this gap, we follow the division of labor in hu- man vision: the periphery examines the whole visual field in parallel at low resolution, whereas high resolution is spent only on the few locations that attention selects [13, 65]. Transferred to kNN search, this principle examines every database vector at low precision in one parallel pass and spends full precision only on the few vectors that the pass cannot exclude. However, a low-precision distance is not exact. Consequently, unless every low-precision decision is certified to be conservative, the pass loses neighbors in the same way as an approximate index. We address this difficulty with a principle that we call certified exclusion: a test may run in any arithmetic as long as it never excludes a vector within the threshold, so that verifying the kept vectors yields the exact neighbors. We realize this principle in an exact search method that we call CertEx. Specifically, CertEx stores a lower-bounding projection of every vector in half precision, together with four coordinates that fold the rounding and accumulation errors [10, 29] of the tensor-core dot product into the prod- uct itself. As a result, one dot product and one comparison per vector decide whether the vector can still be a neighbor, 1 arXiv:2610.21325v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026

By analogy with human vision, we call this half-precision copy of the database the retina and the exact verification of the vectors that it keeps the fovea. Unlike quantization [22, 37] and graph [43, 49] indexes, which decide where a query should look, the retina examines every vector and backs each exclusion by a proof. For instance, Figure 1(a) follows one text query through CertEx: the certified test keeps 274 of the 1,281,167 ImageNet [15] training images, from which the fovea re- turns the exact best matches. By comparison, CAGRA [49] loses the best matching image for the two prompts of Fig- ure 1(b), even at its most accurate configuration. Beyond these examples, CertEx returns exact results on one H100 GPU with 7.1× to 18.0× the throughput of the fastest cuVS [47] fp32 configuration on sixteen datasets, with a speedup that grows with the database size. CertEx also outperforms the GPU indexes IVF-Flat [62], IVF-PQ [37], IVF-RaBitQ [22], and CAGRA [49] whenever every query must be exact. In summary, we make three contributions. • We propose certified exclusion, a new principle for ex- act search that replaces the ranking of all N vectors by one keep-or-exclude decision per vector. Because the decision never excludes a vector within the threshold, even when it runs in half precision, verifying only the kept vectors returns the exact neighbors. • We design CertEx as an exact kNN method that re- alizes certified exclusion on GPU tensor cores [10]. We call its data structure the retina, which is a single half-precision matrix with one row per database vector. Each row holds a lower-bounding projection of one vector and four coordinates of a rounding certificate. We prove that its one-pass tensor-core test never dis- cards a true neighbor, answers range queries and sim- ilarity self-joins (all pairs within a radius) exactly, and keeps survivors between two balls whose gap shrinks as the principal coordinates capture more of the data. • We evaluate CertEx on sixteen datasets with up to 100M vectors, including the embeddings of seven vi- sion encoders such as CLIP [56], DINOv2 [50], and DINOv3 [61]. CertEx answers every query exactly at 7.1× to 18.0× the throughput of the fastest exhaus- tive search of NVIDIA cuVS [47] and is faster than IVF-Flat [62], IVF-PQ [37], IVF-RaBitQ [22], and CAGRA [49] whenever every query must be exact. On the 12.8M web images of DataComp [21], CertEx is exact for every query and finds all 31.4 billion dupli- cate pairs, which makes exact deduplication [1] practi- cal at web scale. 2 Related Work Exact search with lower bounds. Exact methods avoid computing every distance by excluding the vectors whose lower bound exceeds the current neighbor distance. For instance, the k-d tree [7] and the cover tree [9] bound whole regions, whereas AESA [66] bounds single points by the triangle inequality with precomputed pivots. How- ever, the pruning power of such bounds decays with the di- mension [8, 68]. The GEMINI framework [19] therefore moves the bound into a contractive feature space with a proof of no false dismissal, which the VA-file [68] turns into a sequential scan of compact approximations. In con- trast, random projections preserve distances only up to a distortion factor [36] and support only approximate hash- ing [14, 30], whereas exhaustive GPU search [24, 35] avoids bounds altogether. In our terms, GEMINI and the VA-file are certified exclusion tests in full precision whose survivors are still ranked against a running candidate set; in contrast, CertEx certifies a half-precision tensor-core decision inside the same product and replaces the ranking by one compari- son per vector. Approximate indexes. Approximate indexes trade exact- ness for fewer examined vectors. Specifically, product quantization [6, 25, 28, 37] compresses vectors and probes a 2

In addition, FLANN [46] automates the choice among tree and k-means partitions. In contrast, graph in- dexes such as HNSW [43], DiskANN [63], SONG [75], GGNN [26], and CAGRA [49] walk a proximity graph to- ward the query. Benchmarks [5, 60] accordingly rank these methods by recall at a given throughput, whereas CertEx examines every vector and returns exact results. Nearest neighbors in visual recognition. Visual recog- nition uses nearest neighbors as a component whose errors enter the task metric. For instance, object retrieval [3, 32, 53, 62] is evaluated against exhaustive ground truth [55]. Similarly, copy detection [17, 54] and dataset curation [1, 21] remove near and semantic duplicates from web-scale corpora. In representation learning, weighted kNN classi- fiers evaluate self-supervised representations [12, 50, 61]. Retrieval-augmented classification [41] even feeds the re- trieved neighbors into the model. In practice, these pipelines obtain their neighbors from approximate indexes, cluster-restricted comparisons, or kNN graphs of fixed de- gree. In contrast, CertEx returns exact neighbors faster than exhaustive search and answers deduplication with an exact similarity self-join (Section 3.6). Foveation and certified low-precision arithmetic. Vi- sion models allocate resolution unevenly, for instance through recurrent glimpses [45], foveal-peripheral segmen- tation [2], or foveated rendering [27, 31]. Numerical com- puting allocates precision in the same way, for instance in mixed-precision training [44]. Computational geometry goes further: its floating-point filters evaluate a predicate in fast arithmetic together with an error bound [10, 29] and fall back to exact arithmetic only near zero [20, 59]. Following this idea, CertEx folds the error bound into the same half- precision product, so that every low-precision decision of CertEx carries a proof of no false dismissal, unlike approx- imate foveation. 3 Methodology 3.1 Overview Exact kNN search must examine all N database vectors, al- though only the few vectors near the query need full preci- sion. Human vision solves the same problem by dividing its work between two parts of the retina [13] (Figure 2(a)): the periphery covers the whole scene at low resolution, whereas the fovea sees only one spot at full resolution. Our exact kNN method divides its work in the same way (Figure 2(b)). We call this method CertEx, which stands for certified ex- clusion. The left half of Figure 2(b) shows the retina of CertEx, which stores one half-precision vector ˆ x for each of the N database vectors x. We call ˆ x the retina vector of x. The first part of ˆ x keeps a few principal coordinates of x and summarizes the rest by one norm. We call this part the lifted projection of x (Section 3.3). The inner product of two lifted projections determines a lower bound on the distance between their vectors. Although half precision is the fastest arithmetic of GPU tensor cores [10], rounding to half precision can overestimate the distance of a true neigh- bor. To guard against this error, the second part of ˆ x records how large the rounding error of ˆ x can be. We call this part the certificate of ˆ x. With the certificate, the test excludes a vector only if the vector would be excluded even under the worst possible rounding. Moreover, the tensor cores eval- uate this worst case within the same product (Section 3.4). Concretely, a tensor-core pass over the retina keeps a vector x only if ⟨ ˆ q, ˆ x⟩ ≥ θ(q), where the retina vector ˆ q encodes the query q in the same form as ˆ x and the threshold θ(q) follows from an upper bound U on the distance of the k-th nearest neighbor (Section 3.5). Because U is needed before the pass, CertEx obtains it from a few sampled vectors. The test of each vector therefore depends on no other database vector, so that one pass over the retina decides all N vectors without ranking them. We call this pass the retina pass. As Figure 2(b) shows, the pass excludes most vectors (crosses) but never a true neighbor; we call the kept vectors (checks) 3

survivors. The right half of Figure 2(b) shows the fovea, which takes over after the retina pass. For each survivor, the fovea reads the original vector in full precision and computes the exact distance between that vector and the query. As a result, the k survivors with the smallest exact distances are the exact k nearest neighbors of q, marked #1 and #2 for k = 2 in the figure. 3.2 Certified Exclusion Consider a database X := {x 1 , . . . , x N } ⊂ R D and a query q ∈ R D . Exact kNN search returns the index set N k (q) := arg min S⊆[N ],|S|=k P i∈S ∥q − x i ∥, whose far- thest member lies at the distance r k (q) from q. However, computing N k (q) requires exact distances only for the vec- tors that may be neighbors. Definition 1 therefore formal- izes what a test that excludes the other vectors must guaran- tee, whatever arithmetic it uses. Definition 1 (Certified exclusion). A test T (q, x, U ) ∈ {keep, exclude} is a certified exclusion test if its computed output keeps every vector x with ∥q − x∥ ≤ U , for every query q, vector x, and threshold U ≥ 0. Definition 1 constrains only the direction of the errors of a test. Specifically, a certified exclusion test may keep a vector farther than U at the cost of one exact distance, but it never excludes a vector within U . Proposition 1 (Exact search by certified exclusion). For a certified exclusion test T and a threshold U ≥ r k (q), the k vectors with the smallest exact distances among the vectors that T keeps form N k (q). Proof. Every x ∈ N k (q) satisfies ∥q − x∥ ≤ r k (q) ≤ U and is therefore kept by Definition 1. The k smallest exact distances among a superset of N k (q) are the k smallest over X . 3.3 Lifted Lower Bound Proposition 1 leaves open which certified exclusion test to use. CertEx needs a test that reads few bytes, because the retina pass reads every database vector and its cost grows with the number of bytes per vector. CertEx therefore keeps a few principal coordinates of each vector and one more co- ordinate that summarizes the rest, which together still give a lower bound on the distance. Specifically, consider a center c ∈ R D and a matrix V ∈ R m×D whose orthonormal rows are the m leading principal directions of a sample of X . We call m the width of the retina. The lifted projection of a vector keeps its m principal coordinates and summarizes the remaining D − m coordinates by their norm: ℓ(x) :=  V(x − c) ∥(I − V ⊤ V)(x − c)∥  ∈ R m+1 . 3.5 Foveal Verification and Exactness The fovea needs the threshold U before the retina pass and the exact distances of the survivors after it. Before the pass, CertEx samples every s-th retina vector, for a stride s, and scores the sampled vectors by the same computed product b P as the retina pass. Among them, the sampled vectors with the largest products become the anchors A(q). The thresh- old U is then the k-th smallest exact distance among the anchors. Because the anchors are at least k distinct vectors of X , U ≥ r k (q) holds for every query. After the pass, the fovea computes the exact distance of each survivor from the full-precision difference q−x and returns the k smallest per query. Proposition 4 (Exactness). CertEx returns N k (q) for every query q. Proof. Every x with ∥q−x∥ ≤ U satisfies ∥ℓ(q)−ℓ(x)∥ ≤ U by Proposition 2 and survives by Proposition 3. The retina is therefore a certified exclusion test. Since U ≥ r k (q), Proposition 1 yields the claim. The anchors, the rotation V, and the width m therefore influence only the cost of CertEx. For instance, a loose threshold admits more survivors and more exact distances but cannot remove a true neighbor. To quantify this cost, Proposition 5 bounds the number of survivors. For this pur- pose, we write ρ(x) := ∥(I − V ⊤ V)(x − c)∥ for the last coordinate of ℓ(x), which is the norm of the component of x − c that is orthogonal to the rows of V. Similarly, we denote by η(q) the slack that μ(q) and the rounded-up co- ordinates add to the squared threshold, which is of the order of the unit roundoff times the squared norms. Proposition 5 (Survivor ball). Every vector that the retina keeps for the threshold U satisfies ∥q − x∥ 2 ≤ U 2 + η(q) + 4ρ(q)ρ(x). Proof. The proof reuses the notation of the proof of Propo- sition 2. There, u = q − c and v = x − c split as u = u 1 + u 2 and v = v 1 + v 2 , where u 1 , v 1 lie in the row space of V and u 2 , v 2 are orthogonal to it. The norms of u 2 and v 2 are the last coordinates ρ(q) and ρ(x) of the lifted projections. The proof proceeds in three steps. First, the retina keeps x only if its lifted distance is small. By the definition of the slack η(q), every kept vector satis- fies ∥ℓ(q) − ℓ(x)∥ 2 ≤ U 2 + η(q). (17) is at most 4∥u 2 ∥∥v 2 ∥ = 4ρ(q)ρ(x). Adding this bound to Eq. (16) yields ∥q − x∥ 2 ≤ U 2 + η(q) + 4ρ(q)ρ(x), which is the claim. The survivors therefore lie between two balls. Specifi- cally, the inner ball has radius r k (q), and its vectors always survive. In contrast, the outer ball is slightly larger, by an excess that grows with ρ(q) and ρ(x). Because the anchors are the best of every s-th vector, U approximates the dis- tance to the (ks)-th nearest neighbor. The number of sur- vivors thus approaches ks when the width captures most of the variance of the data. A batch of B queries then costs BN (m + 5) half-precision multiply-adds plus about ks ex- act distances per query, whereas exhaustive search costs BN D full-precision multiply-adds and a selection among all N candidates. 3.6 Certified Exclusion at Any Threshold Certified exclusion holds for every threshold, so that CertEx answers any query that fixes its threshold in advance ex- actly and without the anchors. Specifically, Definition 1 and Proposition 3 hold for every U ≥ 0, so that the test of the retina is certified whatever threshold a query uses. The an- chors of Section 3.5 have a different role: they choose the threshold U when a query does not fix it. For instance, kNN search does not fix its threshold, because Proposition 1 re- quires U ≥ r k (q) and the distance r k (q) becomes known only after the search. In contrast, a range query with ra- dius r asks for all database vectors within r of the query, so that its threshold is r from the start. CertEx thus answers a range query by setting U := r, without any anchors. Since the retina may also keep vectors farther than r, the fovea computes their exact distances and removes them. CertEx therefore returns exactly the vectors within r, by Proposi- tions 2 and 3. In particular, near-duplicate detection fixes its threshold in advance as well, because it asks for all pairs of database vectors whose distance is at most a given radius r. We call the set of these pairs the similarity self-join. The self-join therefore consists of the range queries of all database vec- tors against the database, which CertEx answers exactly as above. At 99.9% exact queries (Figure 3(b)), CertEx is 27.2× to 84.9× faster than IVF-Flat [62], 3.7× to 124× faster than IVF-PQ [37], and 2.3× to 10.7× faster than IVF- RaBitQ [22], which is the strongest index on the ImageNet embeddings. In addition, the retina is built in 0.03 to 2.47 seconds, against 2.2 to 29.7 seconds for each CAGRA graph. On the 12.79M DataComp images [21], CertEx is the only method that is exact for every image query. Finally, Figure 3(c) com- pares the survivors of all datasets and BIGANN strides with the estimate ks. Specifically, survivors lie at most 1.15× above ks wherever the width nears the dimension and fur- ther above it for narrow widths (Proposition 5). 4.3 Ablation of the Design Elements We then ask where the speed of CertEx comes from and what its certificate costs, with every element isolated on the same kernel and threshold (Figure 4). For 2048 queries, a complete CertEx search takes 5.0 ms against 37.2 ms for exhaustive search on SIFT1M and 170 ms against 3.6 s on BIGANN-100M, of which the anchors and the fovea take only 2.2 ms and 22 ms (Figure 4(a)). Most of the remain- ing time therefore belongs to the retina pass, which costs less than a plain fp16 matrix multiplication (GEMM) over the same vectors (2.3 ms against 4.1 ms on SIFT1M and 148 ms against 289 ms on BIGANN-100M) because it compares every product with its threshold inside one kernel instead of writing the matrix of all products. In contrast, exhaus- tive search must select the top 100 candidates among all N products, which costs 3.3× to 12.5× the GEMM alone. Moreover, the ablation in Figure 4(b) shows that certified exclusion provides most of the speed: the top-k selection instead slows the pass by 5.6× to 24.3×, whereas TF32 in- stead of fp16 and the width D instead of m slow it by only 1.2× to 1.5× and 1.1× to 2.1×. In addition, the certificate makes the half-precision deci- sion exact (Figure 4(c)). The hardest test places every pair exactly on the decision boundary: for four million random pairs per dataset and width, we set the threshold of each pair to its own lower bound. In this test, the retina keeps ev- ery pair, whereas the same retina without the error terms of Eq. (10) excludes 1.996M to 2.007M of the 4M pairs, be- cause half-precision rounding errs in either direction with equal frequency. Moreover, the largest accumulation error that we measure for 10 8 pairs per dataset and every ker- nel configuration is 0.43% to 0.74% of the certified bound, so that the certificate holds with a margin of more than two orders of magnitude. The certificate costs only 0.4% to 2.7% of throughput, yet it decides real boundary pairs: without it, the exact self-join of the DINOv2 [50] embed- dings misses 299, 50, and 1 duplicate pairs at τ = 0.90, 9

The remaining parameters affect only the cost, so that CertEx stays faster than exhaustive search for every k from 1 to 100 and every batch size from 1 to 4096. 4.4 Vision Encoders We next ask whether the retina stays selective on modern vi- sion encoders (Figure 5). On all seven ImageNet encoders, the retina keeps few survivors, so that CertEx is exact for every query and faster than every baseline at 99.9% exact queries (Figure 5(a)). Moreover, a larger width tightens the bound, so that the survivors per query on DINOv2 [50] fall from 10.3k at m = 507 to 671 at m = 763 (Figure 5(b)). Cross-modal queries further test exactness under a shift of the query distribution, because CLIP [56] text embed- dings occupy a different region of the joint embedding space than the image embeddings [40]. Consequently, IVF- Flat [62] is the only index that reaches 99.9% exact text queries, whereas CertEx is exact for every text query at 41× its throughput (Figure 5(a), right), because certified exclu- sion does not depend on the query distribution. 4.5 Downstream Tasks We finally ask what exact neighbors change in dedupli- cation and kNN classification (Figure 6 and Figure 7). For duplicate detection, the exact self-join of the 1.28M ImageNet [15] training images takes 1.5 to 2.5 seconds, which is 22× to 37× faster than an exhaustive fp32 join, photo 0.998 ✗ photo 0.998 ✗ CertEx RaBitQ king penguin query CertEx RaBitQ gorilla query CertEx: found ✓ SemDeDup: missed ✗ CertEx: found ✓ SemDeDup: missed ✗ (a) deduplication CertEx finds all 40, SemDeDup none CertEx vote: king penguin ✓ RaBitQ vote: killer whale ✗ CertEx vote: gorilla ✓ RaBitQ vote: howler monkey ✗ (b) kNN classifier IVF-RaBitQ turns 463 of 50k correct predictions wrong Figure 7: Real ImageNet examples of both downstream tasks. whereas an exact 10-NN graph contains only 24.6% of its 4.0M pairs at τ = 0.90 (Figure 6(a)). Similarly, SemD- eDup [1] avoids the quadratic join by comparing only the pairs inside each k-means cluster. Measured against the ex- act self-join of CertEx, this restriction misses up to 26% of the pairs of the worst ImageNet classes and up to 66% of all pairs with 50,000 clusters. At web scale, the exact self- join finds all 31.4 billion pairs among 1.97M of the 12.79M DataComp images [21] at τ = 0.95, whereas the cluster restriction cannot detect the duplicates of 41,875 to 56,416 of these images. Similarly, at τ = 0.98, the exact self-join finds all 40 ImageNet images whose copies k-means places in other clusters, whereas SemDeDup with one cluster per class finds none (Figure 7(a)). For the kNN classifier of DINO [12], CertEx returns the exact neighbors of all 50,000 validation images in 0.40 seconds, which is 6.4× faster than the fastest cuVS fp32 configuration (Figure 6(b)). In contrast, the approximate neighbors of IVF-RaBitQ [22] lower the top-1 accuracy of 82.07% by up to 0.42 points, so that a reported kNN ac- curacy also measures the index. Specifically, IVF-RaBitQ turns 463 of the 50,000 correct predictions wrong and only 259 wrong ones correct. For instance, the exact neighbors of a king penguin are king penguins, whereas its approxi- mate ones are killer whales (Figure 7(b)). 5 Conclusion Nearest-neighbor search serves image retrieval and dedu- plication and, increasingly, agentic retrieval and the long- context memory of LLMs. However, exact kNN search has so far required either a full-precision distance to every vec- tor or an index that gives up exactness. CertEx shows that 10

exact search needs neither: a lifted lower bound with a cer- tificate for its rounding error excludes almost every vec- tor in one half-precision tensor-core pass without a false dismissal. On sixteen datasets, including seven vision en- coders and 12.8M web images, CertEx is exact for every query at up to 18.0× the throughput of the fastest exhaustive GPU search. Exact search thus becomes a practical default for image retrieval, web-scale image deduplication, and the evaluation of visual representations.
